paragraphs.text: 13.32. Fees and allowances
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Fees and allowances

paragraphs.text: (1) In every action, application or proceeding in Court, there must be paid to the appropriate court officer or other appropriate person the fee specified, referred to or determined in accordance with Schedule B unless the court clerk waives the fee, in whole or in part, in accordance with guidelines, if any, established or adopted by the Minister of Justice for persons unable to pay fees. (2) Except for fees for transcripts, the fees referred to in subrule (1) are payable in advance unless the court clerk otherwise permits. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 25; 170/2012, s. 10(g); 216/2022, s. 3(2)

(2) Except for fees for transcripts, the fees referred to in subrule (1) are payable in advance unless the court clerk otherwise permits.

paragraphs.text: 13.32. Fees and allowances
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Fees and allowances

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.32:1 Rule 13.32 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.32. 1. Ability To Waive Court Fees In Toronto Dominion Bank v. Beaton, 2012 ABQB 125, 2012 CarswellAlta 369, 534 A.R. 132, 23 C.P.C. (7th) 303, Mr. Beaton sought an order that the Transcript Services of the Government of Alberta provide him, at no charge, transcripts of his court proceedings. The Government submitted that under the Rules only a clerk could waive court fees, and that a judge did not have that authority under the Rules. Justice Veit agreed, but said that she was inclined to the view that judges had the authority waive court fees on the basis of constitutional law (however, her Ladyship acknowledged that the issue is not free from doubt). Though she ultimately denied the order sought, it is respectfully submitted that Justice Veit's comments are most helpful on a difficult issue. After referring to Rules 13.32, and 13.36–13.39, she said, at paragraphs 13–18: 13 In other words, the Rules state that only the clerk has the authority to waive court fees, but provide assistance to litigants of limited financial means by waiving court fees for litigants who have a subsisting Legal Aid Certificate. 14 Given the specificity of Rule 12.32 (sic), I am of the view that a judge cannot circumvent the clear intention of that Rule by using Rule 13.38(1) to grant a fiat ordering the clerk to waive court fees. 15 For ease of reference, Ministerial Order 8/2011, which refers to Rule 12.32 (sic) is reproduced as Appendix A. That M.O identifies which court fees can be waived, and by inference establishes which fees cannot be waived, repeats that it is the court clerk who can waive the fees, and by inference establishes that no one else can waive the fees, and establishes a standard format for the inquiry by the clerk into an applicant's financial circumstances. 16 If the court were only to consider those two pronouncements, the Rules and the Ministerial Order, it would conclude that the court does not have any authority to waive court fees, and that the authority to waive such fees in Alberta resides solely in the Clerk of the Court. 17 However, case law, in particular Polewski, presents an expanded analysis of the issue of the waiver of fees seen through the lens of access to justice. Although that decision deserves careful scrutiny, for the purposes of this application, a fair summary of the Ontario Divisional Court's view of the matter is found in para. 64 of the decision: 64 We agree that Pleau does not stand for the broad proposition that a person has an unrestricted right to recourse to the courts for civil litigation. This is why we emphasize the requirements of proof of indigence and a meritorious claim. We do not suggest that the constitutional right of access to the courts precludes reasonable fees, such as those challenged in this appeal. We do say, however, that in cases where their existence, combined with the requirement to pay them prevents a person from pursuing a meritorious claim, they are unconstitutional. We see this as something that is quite different from the concept that unimpeded or unrestricted access to the civil courts is a constitutionally guaranteed right, a concept that was rejected by Gillese J. (Emphasis added) 18 In other words, Polewski makes a very strong argument that, in some situations, the common law historically, and the Charter today, makes access to justice a constitutional right. The situations where access to justice must be guaranteed are narrow: on the one hand, there must be evidence that the applicant truly cannot afford the required fees. Here, Mr. Beaton has provided no such evidence. On the other hand, the applicant must satisfy the court of the merit of the claim that cannot be advanced without incurring the subject fee. Both aspects of the test must be satisfied before the court has authority to act. Veit, J. then said at paragraph 20: 20 However, with respect, I prefer the formulation of the second part of the test as articulated in Polewski. Before exercising its power to grant access to justice by waiving court fees, the court's obligation is much sterner than the test in Purtle: not only must it decline to intervene where the claim is frivolous, vexatious, or an abuse of process, but it must also decline to intervene unless the applicant has established a meritorious claim. At paragraphs 22–23, she said: 22 In assessing the financial circumstances of the applicant, the court will, of course, take into account the relative ability of the applicant to pay access fees, i.e. the obligation to pay a $600.00 trial fee may well create a different financial burden on a litigant whose only income is social assistance from the burden created on a person who is employed at minimum wage, or on a person who earns above the minimum wage but who has many legal dependents …. 23 In assessing the merits of the case, the court will, presumably, proceed as we do on costs, i.e. consider not the overall merits of the case, but the merits of the particular step in relation to which relief is requested. In other words, rather than trying to forecast if the applicant will be successful in the result, the court should consider whether the applicant's next step has merit.

paragraphs.text: 13.33. Uncertainty of amount of fees and allowances
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Uncertainty of amount of fees and allowances

paragraphs.text: (1) If the amount of a fee, allowance or other amount is uncertain or impossible to determine, the fee or amount may be estimated by the court clerk and adjusted when the fee or amount is fixed by a judge. (2) When a person is paid or given an allowance before actual attendance at an application or proceeding conducted under these rules, the person is entitled to receive any additional sum that is determined to be payable after completion of the attendance. (3) When a party is permitted or required to pay an allowance, that party may have the amount fixed by an assessment officer without notice to any other person, subject to adjustment after completion of the actual attendance.
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: (1) If the amount of a fee, allowance or other amount is uncertain or impossible to determine, the fee or amount may be estimated by the court clerk and adjusted when the fee or amount is fixed by a judge.

(2) When a person is paid or given an allowance before actual attendance at an application or proceeding conducted under these rules, the person is entitled to receive any additional sum that is determined to be payable after completion of the attendance.

(3) When a party is permitted or required to pay an allowance, that party may have the amount fixed by an assessment officer without notice to any other person, subject to adjustment after completion of the actual attendance.

paragraphs.text: 13.35. Fee exemption
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Fee exemption

paragraphs.text: (1) A peace officer is exempt from the payment of fees or other amounts under Schedule B for the search of a name, the inspection of a file or a copy or the certification of a document when the court service is required in the execution or discharge of the peace officer's duties. (2) In this rule, “peace officer” means a peace officer as defined in the Provincial Offences Procedures Act.

paragraphs.text: 13.36. Fee waiver: legal aid
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Fee waiver: legal aid

paragraphs.text: (1) In this rule, (a) “certificate” means a Legal Aid Certificate issued by the Legal Aid Society of Alberta; (b) “document” means any document that may be filed for which a fee is payable under any of items 1 to 4 or 30 to 32.1 of Schedule B. (2) A court clerk who is requested to file a document must waive the filing fee otherwise payable if presented with a subsisting certificate issued in respect of the person for whom the document is to be filed. (3) If a document was filed in an action before a certificate is issued in respect of the person for whom the document was filed, the fee paid for filing the document may not be waived under this rule. (4) A court clerk must waive the fee payable under item 5.1(b) of Schedule B if presented with a subsisting certificate issued in respect of the person owing the fee. Alta. Reg. 216/2011, s. 2; 71/2015, s. 3(2); 36/2020, s. 20

paragraphs.text: 13.37. Fee waiver: restraining orders
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Fee waiver: restraining orders

paragraphs.text: (1) In this rule, “restraining order” means a restraining order in respect of an interpersonal matter between individuals or a protection order under the Protection Against Family Violence Act and includes the costs associated with respect to that restraining order or protection order. (2) If a court clerk files a commencement document or an application in the course of an action or proceeding in which the remedy claimed is a restraining order, the court clerk must waive the fee payable under item 1 or 3.4 respectively of Schedule B. (3) Despite subrule (2), the fee referred to in subrule (2) must not be waived if any remedy, other than or in addition to a restraining order, is being sought in respect of the matter for which the document is being filed. (4) A fee that was waived becomes immediately payable if the party in respect of whom the fee was waived claims or seeks a remedy in respect of the matter other than or in addition to the restraining order. Alta. Reg. 76/2015, s. 3(2)

paragraphs.text: 13.38. Judge's fiat
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Judge's fiat

paragraphs.text: (1) A judge or an applications judge may authorize, direct or give permission to a court officer to do an act, and a note signed by the judge or applications judge is sufficient authority to carry out the act. (2) The authorization, direction or permission must be filed unless the judge or applications judge otherwise directs. Alta. Reg. 136/2022, s. 1(10) 1. The granting of a fiat is discretionary and is owed deference In Waddy v. His Majesty the King in Rights of Alberta (Solicitor General Services Division), 2024 ABCA 408, a chambers justice granted a fiat permitting the late filing of materials. The granting of that fiat was appealed. The Court of Appeal said: [4] The granting of a fiat is a discretionary, procedural decision to which deference is owed on appeal. Rule 13.38 allows a judge to grant a fiat to allow a “court officer to do an [otherwise irregular] act”, including allowing the late filing of documents. A fiat is an order of the court, and the discretion to grant such an order to permit late filing is “essentially a matter of court administration”: Baker v Baker, 2014 ABQB 710 at para 4; R v Ellis, 1995 ABCA 480 at para 3. This Court can only interfere with such a discretionary decision where the chambers judge misdirected herself, the decision is so clearly wrong it amounts to an injustice, or insufficient or no weight is given to relevant considerations: Penner v Niagara (Regional Police Services Board), 2013 SCC 19 at para 27, [2013] 2 SCR 125; Alberta Union of Provincial Employees v Her Majesty the Queen (Alberta), 2021 ABCA 416 at para 13.
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: (1) A judge or an applications judge may authorize, direct or give permission to a court officer to do an act, and a note signed by the judge or applications judge is sufficient authority to carry out the act.

paragraphs.text: 13.39. Court officers
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Court officers

paragraphs.text: The persons holding the following positions are court officers: (a) the court clerk and every person delegated authority by the court clerk or authorized by the court clerk to perform any court clerk functions; (b) the sheriff; (c) a person appointed as a deputy of a person described in clause (a) or (b).

paragraphs.text: 13.41. Authority of court clerk
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Authority of court clerk

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrules (2) and (3), the court clerk must file, issue, certify or do anything with respect to an action, application or proceeding that complies with these rules. (2) The court clerk must not file, issue, certify or do anything with respect to an action, application or proceeding except (a) if sent by electronic means, including by electronic mail, (b) at the written request of the party or person concerned or a person on the party's or person's behalf who completes the prescribed form or other required document and provides it to the court clerk with a prepaid and addressed envelope when return of a document is required, (b.1) if circumstances require, on the personal attendance at the court office by the party or person concerned or a person on that party's or person's behalf, or (c) by a means authorized by the Court. (3) A court clerk may refuse to file, issue, certify or do any other thing with respect to an action, application or proceeding if (a) the instructions to the court clerk are not clear, (b) a document or prescribed form is not satisfactory or not satisfactorily completed, or (c) a requirement of these rules has not been complied with. (4) Notwithstanding subrule (2)(a), where the court clerk has filed an affidavit submitted by electronic means, the party or person who submitted the affidavit for filing must (a) keep the original paper version of the affidavit until the earlier of (i) the date on which the proceeding, including any appeal, is finally disposed of, (ii) the date on which the appeal period for that proceeding has expired if no notice of appeal respecting the proceeding has been filed within that period, and (iii) the date on which the court clerk requests that the original paper version be filed, (b) on request, make the original paper version of the affidavit available for inspection by the other parties or their lawyer and by the Court, and (c) if a request is made under clause (a)(iii), submit the original paper version of the affidavit for filing within 15 days after that request is received. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 26; 194/2020, s. 7

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.41:1 Rule 13.41 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.41. Personal attendance required In Burton v. Burton (1996), 39 Alta. L.R. (3d) 201 (Q.B.), two separate petitioners in divorce actions hired a para-legal (First Choice) to prepare their respective petitions for divorce. The individual petitioners physically took the documents to the court house and filed them. The Law Society claimed that they thereby violated then R. 712. Madam Justice Veit disagreed, and at p. 211 said: The Law Society contends that even though Messrs Burton and West brought their own documents into the courthouse to be filed, they were nevertheless in breach of the Rules: Rule 712 means that the petition was the document of First Choice and not the pleading of Burton and West. I cannot agree. Although I sympathize with the concerns expressed by the Law Society, the wording of the Rules does not extend beyond a literal interpretation. Individuals are entitled to come to the court house to file documents approved by them to be used by them in legal proceedings, whether or not that document has been prepared entirely or partially by some other person.

paragraphs.text: 13.44. Duties of court clerk
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Duties of court clerk

paragraphs.text: In addition to any other duties that a court clerk is required by law to perform, a court clerk has the following duties and responsibilities: (a) to establish and maintain a court file for each action started in the Court and to keep the court file up to date; (b) to receive, file and have custody of all commencement documents, pleadings, affidavits and records filed in every action, application or proceeding; (c) to have custody of all documents required or ordered to be deposited for safekeeping or otherwise under an order or an enactment; (d) to take any action or do anything required or permitted under these rules, an enactment or an order or judgment; (e) in accordance with the Court's directions, to keep a detailed log of court proceedings, including any record that is capable of being represented or reproduced visually or by sound or both and ensure that the recording and log are properly and securely stored; (f) to keep proper accounts and records of money or property received, paid out or disposed of; (g) to perform any other functions required by the Minister or the Chief Justice.
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: In addition to any other duties that a court clerk is required by law to perform, a court clerk has the following duties and responsibilities:
(a) to establish and maintain a court file for each action started in the Court and to keep the court file up to date
(b) to receive, file and have custody of all commencement documents, pleadings, affidavits and records filed in every action, application or proceeding
(c) to have custody of all documents required or ordered to be deposited for safekeeping or otherwise under an order or an enactment
(d) to take any action or do anything required or permitted under these rules, an enactment or an order or judgment

(e) in accordance with the Court's directions, to keep a detailed log of court proceedings, including any record that is capable of being represented or reproduced visually or by sound or both and ensure that the recording and log are properly and securely stored
(f) to keep proper accounts and records of money or property received, paid out or disposed of
(g) to perform any other functions required by the Minister or the Chief Justice.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.44:1 Rule 13.44 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.44. Public Access to Files Having given consideration to the very extensive and learned submissions of both Mr. Cipin and Mr. Malone and having reviewed the relevant authorities and statutes, I return to the four questions placed before me, and state my answers: A. There is no statutory provision compelling a clerk of the court or his deputy to permit public access, including all media, to court files; however, the common law, as recently enlarged by the Supreme Court of Canada in the MacIntyre case, allows public and media access to court files with some exceptions. B. There are only three statutory exceptions, to open access of files, namely, (i) files impounded by order of the court; (ii) solicitor-client contingency fee agreements; and (iii) transcripts of examinations for discovery. At common law the exceptions to public accessibility are based on “the need to protect social values of superordinate importance”, one of which is the protection of the innocent. A further category of exceptions to open access is founded in the administration of justice, i.e., where the administration of justice would be rendered impracticable by the presence of the public. C. Clearly the circumstances surrounding the hostage-taking incident in this case fall within the exception where there is a superordinate need to protect the innocent. There is no doubt whatever that the need to protect the lives and safety of the innocent hostages was of paramount importance and obviously must override the public's accessibility to the court files. D. No, the deputy clerk was not entitled to refuse access to the court files on his own volition, nor on the direction or advice of any of his superior officers in the Attorney General's department. With respect to the filing, custody and control of court files regarding proceedings in court, the clerk is an officer of the court and subject to the jurisdiction of the court, which “has a supervisory and protecting power over its own records”. Thus, the clerk or any person wishing to deny public access to court files must first obtain leave of the court, which may be granted on an application made ex parte. Solomon v. McLaughlin (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 63 (Q.B.), at 77, per Bracco J.

paragraphs.text: 13.45. Notice to be given to court officers
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Notice to be given to court officers

paragraphs.text: (1) Every party or person (a) who receives an order or judgment, or (b) in whose favour an order or judgment is made that imposes duties on a court officer must give to the court officer written notice of the order or judgment and of the duty imposed under the order or judgment unless the Court otherwise orders. (2) Filing the order or judgment is not notice to the court officer.

paragraphs.text: 13.46. Official court reporters
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Official court reporters

paragraphs.text: (1) An official court reporter must perform the duties required under these rules or assigned by the Minister or the Court and must (a) keep in safe custody the record of any proceedings or questioning taken by the official court reporter, (b) honestly and accurately transcribe the record of those proceedings or that questioning, and (c) deliver a copy of the transcript as required by these rules. (2) On or attached to a transcript, the official court reporter must (a) state the official court reporter's name, (b) specify the date and place where the proceedings or questioning occurred, and (c) certify the transcript, or the portion of the transcript transcribed, as complete and accurate. Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 27

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 13.46:1 Rule 13.46 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 13.46. 1. Duty of Confidentiality In Ritter v. Hoag (2004), 50 Alta. L.R. (4th) 242 (Q.B.), Burrows J. concluded that court reporters are bound by a duty of confidentiality in relation to evidence given at examinations for discovery. At p. 248, his Lordship said: In my view, an official court reporter must have a duty of confidentiality in respect of discovery evidence. Otherwise the implied undertaking to which the litigants and their counsel are bound would be ineffective. In the absence of any statement to that effect in the Rules or in any other authority I have been able to find, and since, in this case, there is a particular need for clarity as it may be necessary to establish the obligations of the Alberta court reporter in a U.S. court, an order requiring that discovery evidence be kept confidential by court officers, including the court reporter who records the discovery, should be granted, even though the confidentiality duty exists without it being ordered. 2. Presumption of Regularity Applies With respect to the transcripts we refer to rule 729 of the Rules of Court… Here the principle of omnia presumuntur rite esse acta applies The allegations with respect to inaccuracies in the tapes and transcript are based purely on the memory and recollection of the appellant and Stephen Horne and on the appellant's interpretation of what he alleges he heard when he listened to the tapes in March 1986. This is not sufficient to displace the prima facie presumption of the regularity of the transcripts. R. v. Horne (1987), 78 A.R. 78 at 80 (C.A.). Omnia presumuntur[sic]rite esse acta: “A prima facie presumption of the regularity of the acts of public officers exists until the contrary appears.” Black's Law Dictionary, 6th ed., (1990, West Publishing Co.), at p. 1087.

paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: How money is paid into Court

paragraphs.text: (1) Money paid into Court must be paid to the court clerk and accompanied with Form 50. (2) The court clerk must (a) give a receipt for money paid into Court, and (b) deposit the money in an account in a bank, treasury branch or trust corporation, unless otherwise ordered.

paragraphs.text: 13.50. Tender on judicial sale
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Tender on judicial sale

paragraphs.text: (1) Certified cheques received by the court clerk as a tender on a judicial sale must be held by the court clerk on behalf of the person making the tender. (2) If the court clerk expects the tender to be considered by the Court or otherwise dealt with within one month after receipt of the certified cheque, the court clerk may hold the cheque without depositing it. (3) If the court clerk expects that a tender will not be considered or otherwise dealt with within one month after receipt of the certified cheque, or if the person making the tender so requests within one month after making the tender, the court clerk must invest the money in securities described in rule 13.54.

paragraphs.text: 13.52. Payments into Court under Trustee Act
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Payments into Court under Trustee Act

paragraphs.text: (1) An application for permission to pay money or securities into Court under the Trustee Act or a payment into Court under that Act must be accompanied with an affidavit of one or more trustees setting out (a) a brief description of the trust, the instrument or enactment creating it or the circumstances under which it arose, (b) the name of every person interested in or entitled to the money or securities, together with their addresses, if known, and (c) an address for service of documents. (2) Notice of the application or payment into Court must be given to every person that the Court orders be notified.

paragraphs.text: 13.53. Payments out of Court
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Payments out of Court

paragraphs.text: Money paid into Court may be paid out of Court only (a) if the court clerk certifies that the money is in Court, (b) in accordance with an order, unless otherwise permitted by the Court, (c) by cheque signed and countersigned by a person designated by the Minister, and (d) if the payment is to (i) the person entitled to the money or the person's lawyer, or (ii) another person specified by the Court or named by the person entitled to the money.

paragraphs.text: 13.54. Investments and payment earnings
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Investments and payment earnings

paragraphs.text: (1) Money paid into Court or money subject to an order may be invested on the court clerk's initiative or on the written request of a person having an interest in the money, and if the money is invested, the money may only be invested in (a) public funds of Alberta or Canada, (b) deposit certificates of a bank, treasury branch or trust corporation, or (c) securities or a class of securities authorized by the Court. (2) Money earned on investments made under subrule (1) must be paid to the person entitled to the money paid into Court when the principal amount is paid out, unless the Court otherwise orders.

paragraphs.text: 13.55. Disposition of money in accounts
paragraphs.heading: Part 13. Technical Rules

sentences.text: Disposition of money in accounts

paragraphs.text: (1) If the balance remaining to the credit of a court account is less than $100 and 2 years has passed after the amount was deposited in the account without the balance being claimed, the account must be closed by transferring the balance to the suspense account maintained by the court clerk. (2) Subject to subrule (1), 10 years after the last payment into a court account, the balance must be transferred to the suspense account. (3) Money in the suspense account, including interest or any return on money in that account, is subject to the control of, and may be paid out only in accordance with a direction of, the Lieutenant Governor in Council. (4) This rule does not affect the right of a person entitled to the money in the suspense account, including the right to recover the money.
